Confidence: secure = in the top 10 in at least 80% of 1,000 match resamples; probable = 50–80%; marginal = below 50%. Rating: 50 = average eligible player; higher is better. Team = IPL 2026 franchise.

The method in four lines

  1. Pressure = leverage. A win-probability model built on this data tells us how far one ball can swing the match. The top 25% of balls by that swing in each innings are pressure balls; a first-innings pressure ball counts 0.53 of a chase one, in proportion to what is at stake.
  2. Performance = Impact. The win probability a player adds on a ball, divided by what was at stake, compared with the league average in the same situation.
  3. Rating = level, shift and consistency. 60% pressure level, 15% change from the player's usual level, 25% share of pressure matches won for the team, after shrinking small samples towards the average.
  4. Checks. Rank intervals from 1,000 match resamples, a 2022–24 → 2025–26 time split, and 13 alternative versions of the method.

Three findings

  1. The usual definition of pressure measures the wrong balls. "Death overs, or a required rate above 10" misses 54% of the high-leverage balls in chases, and 59% of the chase balls it does flag are dead or below-median leverage.
  2. Pressure balls really are different, but not everywhere. Comparing like with like (same over, same wickets down), chasing batters score 8 strike-rate points slower on middle-overs pressure balls. In the first innings, "pressure" is mostly the new ball and carries about half the stake, so it counts about half, and each pick's chase-only rank is shown too.
  3. Bowlers' pressure form partly repeats; batters' does not. Rated on 2022–24, bowlers' pressure level correlates 0.24 with their 2025–26 pressure Impact (full rating 0.19); for batters the rating's correlation is 0.03. The bowling list is the firmer of the two; the batting list ranks who has delivered, not a forecast.

How sure we are: 2 batters and 2 bowlers are secure; 3 and 3 are marginal, and places 9–10 are close to coin-flips against 11–12. Every number in this report is read from a file the pipeline writes to outputs/.

1. Pressure definition Brief item: which situations and indicators, and why

1.1 A win-probability model built on this data

Pressure starts from win probability (WP): the chance that the batting side wins, given the score, balls left, wickets in hand and, in a chase, the target. We fit it on 180,910 balls from 758 completed matches. Associate T20Is, DLS-affected games, ties and no-results are left out of fitting (their outcomes are mismatches or unreliable) but are still scored.

  • First innings: a logistic regression on how far the projected total sits above par. Par is the average first-innings total in the same competition tier and season, leaving the match itself out, which tracks the rise in IPL scoring year by year.
  • Chase: a logistic regression on how many runs the chasing side is ahead of an average side with the same balls and wickets left.
  • Last 6 balls of a chase: the regression misjudges the final over, so WP is computed exactly by playing out every remaining ball with league outcome rates for the same runs-per-ball requirement, fully so on the last ball.
InningsBrierBrier, constant guessAUCCalibration error
First innings0.2200.2500.700.018
Chase0.1160.2490.920.007

Brier = mean squared error of the predicted probability (lower is better; the constant guess predicts the average win rate). Calibration error = average gap between predicted and actual win rates over ten probability bins, on matches the model never saw (5-fold cross-validation by match).

Sanity checks (chasing side with 5 wickets in hand): 6 needed off the last ball, WP 0.13; 4 off the last ball 0.24; 12 off 3 0.11; 6 off 6 0.96; 30 off 6 0.01.

The chase model is strong (AUC 0.92). The first-innings model is weaker (AUC 0.70): before the chase starts, much of the result is still unknown. First-innings leverage inherits that, which is one reason we report a chase-only rank for every pick.

1.2 Leverage: how much one ball can swing the match

For every ball we compute the WP after each of 8 possible outcomes (dot, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, wicket, extra), weight them by how often each happens in that innings and phase, and take their spread (standard deviation). Dividing by the all-ball average gives the Leverage Index (LI): an average ball is 1.00; a ball with LI 3 carries three times the usual stake. The 95th percentile is 2.29, the 99th 3.84, and the highest, the last ball of a close chase, 17.7.

1.3 Pressure balls

A pressure ball is one whose LI is at or above the 75th percentile of its own innings, so 25% of the balls in each innings qualify (49,718 in all). A dead ball cannot move WP by more than 0.2 points; these (6.2% of balls, mostly lost causes) are dropped, so runs in a dead game count for nothing. Everything else is a routine ball.

Why the cut is set within each innings. Chase leverage is either near zero or very high, while first-innings leverage is flat. One league-wide cut would make 98% of pressure balls chase balls, and nobody would be rated on setting a total. So pressure is measured relative to the job, and we show the split openly.

InningsLI cutMedian LI of pressure ballsPowerplay %Middle %Death %
First innings1.041.1577211
Chase1.712.17265025

How much each innings counts. The two kinds of pressure ball do not carry the same stake: the median pressure ball has LI 1.15 in the first innings and 2.17 in a chase. So in the rating a first-innings pressure ball counts 0.53 of a chase pressure ball (the ratio of the two medians). First-innings play is still rated, but the new ball cannot outweigh a tight chase. The ratio is measured, not chosen, and was fixed before any re-ranking; equal weights are variant V13 (section 5.3).

What first-innings pressure is. It is mostly the new ball: 98% of first-over balls and 84% of second-over balls are pressure balls, and first-innings powerplay balls are 40% of all pressure balls. Early wickets move the projected total most, so that is where the first-innings stakes are, but they are only mildly high (median LI 1.15 against 2.17 in chases). Chase pressure sits in close games: 88% of chase pressure balls come with WP between 20% and 80%.

1.4 Evidence that pressure balls matter

Phase alone is not enough. Mean absolute WP change per ball, in percentage points: the death overs move WP more than the middle overs, but the leverage bands separate balls far more sharply than phase does.

By phase

1.421.151.66
By leverage band
Low (bottom 50%)MediumPressureCrunch (top 5%)
0.791.481.674.97

Outcomes change on pressure balls, like for like. Figure 3 compares pressure and routine balls inside the same over and the same number of wickets down, so the gap is not just "later overs" or "more wickets down". The crude gaps (hollow circles) are mostly that mix. What holds: chasing batters score 8.1 strike-rate points slower on middle-overs pressure balls (90% interval 4.6 to 11.7 slower) and 5.1 slower in the powerplay, where the interval just reaches zero. At the chase death there is no strike-rate gap and the wicket gap (+0.7 points) is not clear of zero. In first-innings middle overs, batters score faster on pressure balls (+10.6). We report this mixed picture as found: pressure changes the game, and players differ in how they respond, which is what the rating measures.

The usual definition misses most pressure balls. In chases, "overs 16–20 or required rate above 10" misses 54% of our pressure balls and 36% of crunch balls (top 5% of LI), while 59% of the balls it flags are dead or below-median leverage.

2. Performance measurement Brief item: batting and bowling metrics, baselines, rating logic

2.1 Value of one ball: Impact

Impact = (WP after the ball − WP before) ÷ leverage of the ball − league average for the same situation

Impact is how much a ball helped the team's win chances, measured against how much was at stake on it, compared with what an average player does in the same situation. Raw WP added is larger on pressure balls simply because more is at stake; dividing by leverage puts pressure and routine balls on one scale, so the two can be compared. Impact is split into a run part (the WP change without the wicket) and a wicket part, each capped at ±6 so one freak ball cannot dominate. Figures are per 100 balls; positive helps the player's team.

  • Batter: the run part on every ball faced, and the wicket part only when he is out. Wides are not the striker's; a non-striker run-out is charged to nobody.
  • Bowler: every delivery, wides and no-balls included, with the sign flipped; the wicket part only for bowler wickets (not run-outs).
  • Centring: from each ball we subtract the league-average credited Impact in the same innings, over group (1–2, 3–6, 7–10, 11–15, 16–18, 19–20) and pressure flag. Without this, openers looked worse and new-ball bowlers better under pressure purely because of where they play: eligible batters' average shift was −3.1 per 100 balls before centring and −0.3 after; bowlers' +2.6 and −0.4.

2.3 Baseline: the player's own routine balls

A player's usual level is his Impact on his own routine balls (neither pressure nor dead), in the same tiers with the same weights. Routine rather than all balls, so the two sides of the comparison do not overlap.

2.4 The rating

SymbolComponentDefinition
UUsual levelImpact per 100 routine balls; run and wicket parts shrunk separately.
DPressure shiftPressure Impact minus routine Impact, shrunk towards the pool average shift.
P = U + DPressure levelBest estimate of the player's Impact per 100 pressure balls.
CConsistencyShare of pressure matches (≥ 3 pressure balls) in which the player's pressure WPA was positive, shrunk towards the pool rate.
Rating = 60% · z(pressure level) + 15% · z(shift) + 25% · z(consistency),   reported as 50 + 10 × rating

Each z-score divides the player's shrunk value by the spread of the raw values across the pool. A component that the data cannot measure well is pulled close to the average by shrinkage (section 3.1), so it ends up with little spread and counts for little. The weights were fixed before any ranking was seen; the effective weights below show how much each component actually moves the ranking.

Weight % (nominal / effective)
ListLevelShiftConsistency
Batters60 / 7715 / 1125 / 13
Bowlers60 / 8715 / 225 / 11

Why level leads. Pressure level is what wins matches and is the best-measured component. The shift is the brief's "compared with their usual level", but it is the difference of two noisy numbers, so for bowlers it is shrunk almost to zero (shrunk shifts range −1.4 to +0.4 per 100 balls, against −7.0 to +6.6 for batters). Never the drop alone: a player who is poor in every situation has no drop at all, so ranking on the drop would reward him.

3. Fair comparisons Brief item: sample sizes, eligibility, match context, IPL + T20I

3.1 Shrinking small samples (empirical Bayes)

Each estimate is pulled towards the pool average by an amount set by the data: shrunk = average + n ÷ (n + k) × (raw − average), where n is the player's effective number of balls. k is the number of balls at which we trust the player's own record as much as the league average, estimated from how much players really differ compared with ball-to-ball noise. Run and wicket parts are shrunk separately because wickets take far longer to settle. Priors and k are estimated on players with at least 200 balls and 60 pressure balls.

QuantityBattersBowlers
Usual level, run part189255
Usual level, wicket part510980
Pressure shift4795,000 (cap)
Consistency (pseudo-matches)79116

"Cap" = the data shows almost no real spread between bowlers' shifts, so k hits the 5,000-ball ceiling and the shift is close to the average for everyone.

3.3 Combining IPL and T20I data

Two separate adjustments. A difficulty offset is measured: for players with at least 150 balls both in a tier and in the IPL, the average difference in their Impact, taken off every ball in that tier. A relevance weight is a judgment, fixed in advance: the target is IPL 2027, so IPL evidence counts most. Associate and Emerging offsets are zero because fewer than 15 players qualify; for those tiers the low weights do the work.

TierRelevance weightOffset, batters (Impact/100)Offset, bowlers (Impact/100)

Half-life of 2 years, applied to every ball and match.

  • Era and competition: par is set per competition tier and season, so a 190 in IPL 2026 is judged against IPL 2026, including the deeper batting since the Impact Player rule.
  • Situation: Impact is centred on innings, over group and pressure flag (2.1).
  • Venue: not adjusted; the data has anonymous venue ids only.
  • Opposition: no explicit adjustment beyond competition tier (see limitations).

5. Reliability and limitations Brief item: consistency across matches, uncertainty

5.1 How sure is each place?

We resample whole matches 1,000 times and re-rank. 2 batters and 2 bowlers stay in the top 10 in at least 80% of resamples. The order inside a confidence band is the point estimate only, and places 9–10 are close to coin-flips: #11 Andre Russell is top 10 in 40% of resamples and #11 Abrar Ahmed in 33%. The intervals hold the WP model and shrinkage settings fixed, so the true uncertainty is larger.

5.2 Does pressure form repeat?

We rate players on 2022–24 only and check how well each measure predicts their raw pressure Impact in 2025–26 (players with at least 75 pressure balls in both periods). Because the 2025–26 outcome is itself noisy, no predictor could exceed about 0.54 for batters and 0.48 for bowlers (split-half reliability). For bowlers, pressure level (0.24, 90% interval +0.02 to +0.44) recovers a fair part of what is recoverable; the full rating (0.19, −0.03 to +0.39) less clearly. For batters, the rating shows no persistence (+0.03, 90% interval −0.16 to +0.23); raw pressure Impact (0.18) and the usual death-overs strike rate (0.20) do slightly better, but their intervals overlap zero and each other. We did not retune the weights on about 60 players. The batting list is the best evidence of who has delivered, not a forecast.

Each variant changes one choice and re-ranks the same pool. 5 batters and 8 bowlers stay top 10 in at least 10 of 13 variants ("core picks"; the "Variants top 10" column in section 4). The biggest changes come from a single league-wide pressure cut (V3, which in practice rates chases only), ranking on raw WP added instead of Impact (V12), dropping the recency weights (V7) and IPL balls only (V9). Counting both innings' pressure balls equally (V13) keeps 9 of 10 batters and 10 of 10 bowlers.

Consistency across matches. Raw pressure WPA is dominated by a handful of last-over balls, so it can disagree with Impact. For bowlers it does: Jasprit Bumrah's pressure WPA is +0.22 wins in total and −0.15 without his best match; Lungi Ngidi's is −0.64. Every pick's three best and three worst pressure matches are in outputs/top10_match_detail.csv.

5.4 Limitations

  • Batting persistence. The batter rating does not predict the next period (5.2). Treat batting places beyond the secure ones as a record of delivery.
  • Small samples. Vaibhav Sooryavanshi's evidence is almost all from one season; Priyansh Arya is close to the career-volume minimum (446 balls). Both are flagged in Table 3.
  • IPL evidence. Mohammad Nawaz has 0 IPL pressure balls and Finn Allen 38; their ratings rest mainly on T20Is, adjusted by an offset measured on the players who play in both (Table in 3.3) and down-weighted.
  • First-innings pressure is mostly the new ball, and the first-innings WP model is weaker (AUC 0.70). The chase-only rank in section 4 shows who also holds up when chasing.
  • Last ball of a chase. After the exact play-out, the model is still slightly pessimistic there on average (+1.9 WP points per ball, standard error 1.1, 253 balls).
  • Role effects. Centring removes most of the effect of where a player bats; the correlation between batters' role mix and their shift falls from 0.38 to 0.27, not to zero.
  • No venue or opposition adjustment. Venue names are missing (anonymous ids only), and opposition strength is only handled through competition tiers.
  • DLS and short games. 4 DLS games have no revised target, so their chases are not scored; DLS games are left out of fitting; other revised targets are taken from the data.
  • Accounting simplifications. Byes and leg-byes sit inside the run part for both batter and bowler. Super overs are excluded; 9 tied matches are scored with a level finish worth 0.5.

A. Reproducing the results

B. Full eligibility rules

  • Scored balls: innings 1–2 of completed and tied matches; no-result and abandoned games, super overs and the chases of the 4 DLS games without a revised target are excluded. Live balls are scored balls that are not dead.
  • Batters count balls faced (wides excluded); bowlers count legal deliveries. All four tiers count towards eligibility.
  • Career ≥ 400 live balls; ≥ 125 pressure balls; ≥ 10 pressure matches (a match with at least 3 pressure balls); ≥ 60 live balls in 2025–2026.
  • Shrinkage priors and k: players with ≥ 200 live balls and ≥ 60 pressure balls. Time split: ≥ 75 pressure balls in each period.

D. Decision log summary

DecisionWhat we chose, and the alternative we rejected
D1–D5Standard scoring rules: legal ball, bowler charges, bowler wickets, chase target from revised target or first-innings total; four competition tiers.
D6–D8, D25–D27WP model = two logistic regressions on an expected-runs curve, par by tier × season; trained on completed non-DLS, non-associate matches, calibration judged out of fold. Rejected: gradient boosting (stepped surface), venue effects.
D35Last six chase balls: exact play-out blended with the regression. Rejected: one outcome mix for all requirements.
D9–D10, D41, D45Leverage Index; pressure = top share of LI within each innings; first-innings pressure balls weighted by the ratio of median pressure LI (D45). Rejected: one global cut (rates chases only), phase rules.
D11–D13, D36Impact = WP added ÷ leverage, centred on innings × over group × pressure flag; routine balls as baseline. Rejected: raw WPA as the rated quantity (kept as a variant).
D14–D17, D37Pressure level = usual level + shrunk shift; consistency = shrunk share of positive pressure matches; weights fixed in advance; z-scores on raw spread. Rejected: ranking on the drop alone; tuning weights on the time split.
D18–D21, D38Empirical-Bayes shrinkage; eligibility minimums on all tiers; measured tier offsets plus fixed relevance weights; two-year recency half-life. Rejected: an IPL-ball minimum; weights alone.
D22No explicit opposition adjustment (circular and thin). Stated as a limitation.
D23, D39–D40, D42–D44Reliability: match bootstrap with confidence bands, time split reported as found with a noise ceiling, within-cell validation, match-level detail and high-variance flags.
Q1–Q2Data-only ranking (no RR adjustment); super overs excluded.
